config.prompt: How 10 million ballots got it wrong — order the chain:
items: Draw the sample from telephone directories and car registrations during the Depression
Mail 10 million ballots and collect 2.4 million responses — self-selection in who replied
Roosevelt wins by one — coverage bias had selected the affluent
config.why: George Gallup called the election within a few points using a few thousand properly chosen respondents — a small, honest random beats a vast, biased one.

activities.caption: true or false — the big sample's promise
activities.name: doeBiasJudge

statements.s: A bigger sample fixes a biased one.
statements.why: Bias is systematic; size only shrinks random error. Ten million biased ballots said Landon.

statements.s: More data from the wrong mechanism makes you more precisely wrong — and more confident about it.
statements.why: Precision about the wrong thing is worse than honest noise.

statements.s: The Literary Digest sample failed because it was too small.
statements.why: 2.4 million responses — enormous and wrong: coverage bias compounded by self-selection.

statements.s: A representative sample is defined by its selection mechanism, not by looking typical.
statements.why: Hand-picking a 'typical-looking' group reintroduces judgment and its biases; the mechanism must give everyone a known chance of inclusion.

activities.anchor: The classic failure modes have names
activities.caption: file each survey defect
activities.name: doeSurveySort

config.prompt: Bad instruments read zero — file each failure mode:

items.label: 'improve safety and reduce waste' — which half?
general trust in journalism asked before a specific outlet changes the answer
everyone reports more reading and less drinking than is true
about a quarter of respondents offer opinions on fictitious policies

config.why: Design discipline: pilot the instrument, keep items single-barrelled and neutral, randomise option order, and record refusals — 'don't know' is data, not noise.

activities.anchor: The classification is a property of the measurement
activities.caption: pair each variable with its data type
activities.name: doeDataMatch

config.prompt: Match each variable to the data it yields:

pairs.right: continuous — any value in an interval
nominal — despite looking numeric, it is a property of the measurement, not the storage format

config.why: A mean of ordinal ratings is a category error — medians and modes are the honest summaries, and bar charts (never histograms) belong to categorical data.

activities.caption: run the power calculation's bottom line
activities.name: doePowerEst

config.prompt: Detect a 5-point improvement, SD 15, 80% power at 0.05 two-sided. Roughly how many per group does the calculation demand?
config.why: n = 2(z₀.₉₇₅ + z₀.₈₀)²·σ²/Δ² = 2 × 7.84 × 9 ≈ 141 — about 142 per arm. Run 20 and the most likely outcome is a noisy non-result that wastes the study.
config.context: Replication is the pillar that turns a comparison into an error estimate.

activities.caption: who gets group B? — run the allocation
activities.name: doeAllocBranch

config.root: Twenty pupils, two arms, one new teaching method. Someone has to decide who gets it.

choices.label: The teacher assigns by judgment, whoever seems fair
choices.feedback: Haphazard is human choice in disguise — predictable, and therefore biased by the chooser.

choices.label: A concealed computer allocation, performed after enrolment
choices.feedback: Nobody can steer who gets what — unknown confounders distribute between the arms in expectation.

choices.label: Alternate B, A, B, A down the register
choices.feedback: Deterministic — anyone who knows the register can predict the next arm. Allocation concealment is the point.

haphazard.text: The chooser's biases ride into the arms — matching and adjusting control only the confounders you thought of.

concealed.text: The only mechanism that controls unknown confounders — the comparison is fair in expectation.

alternating.text: Predictable assignment is steerable assignment — the leak the protocol exists to close.

config.why: The distance between 'put that one in group B' and 'the computer assigned that one to B' is the entire discipline.

activities.anchor: Assemble the whole apparatus on a real-scale question
activities.caption: one decision in this trial is wrong — click it
activities.name: doeTrialSpot

config.prompt: One decision in this app trial is wrong — click it:
lines: Sampling frame: schools that volunteer — a frame bias, acknowledged in the write-up rather than hidden.
Stratify the frame by catchment type and draw 34 schools.
Randomise individual pupils within each school, to avoid cluster effects.
Pre-register the primary endpoint: a standardised machine-marked test, same date for every pupil.
Apply blinding where it can be — marking and analysis.
config.correction: Cluster-randomise the schools, 17 per arm — the app deploys class by class, and individual randomisation would leak across desks.
config.why: Every decision was made before the first data point existed — which is the chapter's whole argument compressed into one page.

activities.caption: well-powered vs underpowered — drag the divider
activities.name: doePowerCompare

config.prompt: Two literatures, same nominal 5% — drag the divider:

before.label: the well-powered trial
before.text: estimates land close to the truth; the significant results do not have to be lucky

after.label: the underpowered trial
after.text: among significant results, only lucky overestimates clear the bar — effect sizes inflate (the winner's curse) and the false discovery rate climbs

config.why: Across a literature, low prior odds plus underpowering guarantee a false discovery rate far above the nominal 5% — Ioannidis 2005's argument, answered by pre-registration, replication and pre-set stopping rules.
